contract: Only words, individual forms and English grammar/scenarios are prescribed. Every instructional Pashto clause is compiled; no sentence targets or authored fallbacks.

residential.name: Your Home
residential.intro: Doors, rooms, family and everyday actions.

days.title: It / Things
days.intro: Muhammad Jan welcomes you and prepares your home handover.
days.challenge: Muhammad Jan welcomes you and prepares your home handover.
grammar: A description places a noun before an adjective and a present equative. Choose the equative and adjective form that agree with the noun. Feminine singular, masculine singular and inherent plural nouns have different agreement.

days.title: He / She
days.intro: Ms Hameed demonstrates actions at School before your village visits.
days.challenge: Ms Hameed demonstrates actions at School before your village visits.
grammar: A present action clause normally puts the subject first, the object next and the complete finite verb last. Third-person singular verbs describe he, she or one named person. Learn each evidenced conjugation as a complete form.

days.title: I
days.intro: Saleha practises talking about yourself; Edris helps you shop for dinner.
days.challenge: Saleha practises talking about yourself; Edris helps you shop for dinner.
grammar: Use the first-person singular pronoun to speak as I. Select the evidenced first-person singular present verb, rather than adding an ending to an unknown stem.

days.title: You (informal)
days.intro: Muhammad Jan invites a friendly conversation at Home.
days.challenge: Muhammad Jan invites a friendly conversation at Home.
grammar: Address one familiar friend with the informal singular second person. Keep the finite verb in second-person singular. Whole clauses can be linked only when both clauses are licensed.

days.title: You (polite/plural)
days.intro: Ms Hameed explains respectful address before the lakeside gathering.
days.challenge: Ms Hameed explains respectful address before the lakeside gathering.
grammar: Use respectful or plural second person for elders, teachers or a group. Its present verb form differs from familiar singular you. The speaker and addressee are different roles.

days.title: We
days.intro: Saleha introduces her sister Mina; you join them for a walk in the Hills.
days.challenge: Saleha introduces her sister Mina; you join them for a walk in the Hills.
grammar: First-person plural includes the speaker. Contrast we with a group you are addressing. Whole attested coordinated subjects and compound predicates remain intact.

days.title: They
days.intro: Edris describes the shoppers; Ms Hameed conducts the Week 1 examination.
days.challenge: Edris describes the shoppers; Ms Hameed conducts the Week 1 examination.
grammar: Third-person plural describes an observed group outside the speaker and listener. A written present form may be shared with third-person singular; the subject still distinguishes the group.

days.title: This One or That One?
days.intro: Saleha describes nearby and distant objects at the lakeside; player identifies intended objects and constructs demonstrative sentences.
days.challenge: Saleha describes nearby and distant objects at the lakeside; player identifies intended objects and constructs demonstrative sentences.
grammar: Near and far demonstratives can point to an object or stand independently. Keep their deictic function separate from the personal pronoun with the same spelling. Adjectives inside a noun phrase precede the noun.

days.title: One, Two, Many
days.intro: Edris takes inventory; match quantities to item groups, interpret singular/plural, and assemble agreement-safe sentences.
days.challenge: Edris takes inventory; match quantities to item groups, interpret singular/plural, and assemble agreement-safe sentences.
grammar: Use only the studied direct plural of each noun. Agreement follows the actual number and gender. Count expressions require an evidenced numeral construction; missing numeral or noun forms stay unavailable.

days.title: Where Is Mina’s Notebook?
days.intro: Mina retraces her route. Questions describe locations; the player interprets clues to identify the notebook’s location through dialogue only.
days.challenge: Mina retraces her route. Questions describe locations; the player interprets clues to identify the notebook’s location through dialogue only.
grammar: Describe locations with studied here/there forms or complete case-governed spatial expressions. A direct-case noun is not automatically an oblique form. A where question requires a compatible location response.

days.title: Whose Things Are These?
days.intro: Muhammad Jan sorts misplaced possessions after a visit; the player identifies owners in an everyday conversation.
days.challenge: Muhammad Jan sorts misplaced possessions after a visit; the player identifies owners in an everyday conversation.
grammar: Keep owner and owned head distinct. Independent possessives and named oblique possession chunks are studied separately. The described or identified noun determines its own agreement.

days.title: Ask the Right Question
days.intro: A short classroom interview led by Ms Hameed; select suitable questions and respond using familiar vocabulary.
days.challenge: A short classroom interview led by Ms Hameed; select suitable questions and respond using familiar vocabulary.
grammar: Choose a question for a person, object, choice, location, owner or count. A generated reply must answer the question with the same referent and grammatical roles.

days.title: How We Do Things
days.intro: Saleha and Mina plan a routine walk around town; identify how/when actions take place and form meaningful sentences with adverbs.
days.challenge: Saleha and Mina plan a routine walk around town; identify how/when actions take place and form meaningful sentences with adverbs.
grammar: Adverbs express time, manner, frequency or joint action. Their meaning must suit the predicate. Keep the evidenced finite verb and its subject agreement.

days.title: The Village Scavenger Hunt
days.intro: Week 2 culminating challenge: Ms Hameed reviews 25 contextual prompts framed as village scavenger-hunt clues (20/25 to pass), with cumulative Week 1 integration.
days.challenge: Week 2 culminating challenge: Ms Hameed reviews 25 contextual prompts framed as village scavenger-hunt clues (20/25 to pass), with cumulative Week 1 integration.
grammar: Combine previously studied vocabulary and grammar. This is revision: no compulsory new word or form is introduced.
